title: Making Distillation Cheap: Offline Top-K Logits and a Fused Chunked KL Loss
hook: You don't need the teacher in memory. Cache its top-K logits once, then train the student against the cache — same loss, ~29% faster per step, and 4x the context on one GPU.
key_points: Small models are usually compressed then 'healed' via knowledge distillation, and that recovery step largely decides final quality.
Offline KD caches the teacher's top-K logits once, so the teacher never occupies GPU memory during student training.
The authors report offline KD matching online distillation at near-identical training loss.
Offline KD runs about 29% faster per iteration and reaches up to 41% higher throughput on a single H200.
A fused, chunked KL loss never materializes the full vocabulary-sized logit tensor, making peak memory linear in sequence length.
That removes the memory spike capping context, enabling 32,768-token training on one GPU; the chunked-loss code is released.
content_html: If you need a language model that fits tight latency, cost, or on-premises constraints, you probably won't train it from scratch — you'll compress a bigger one and then heal it with knowledge distillation. That healing step is where most of the final quality comes from, and it is expensive. A practitioner's study from the CompactifAI team asks a plain engineering question: how do you make it cheap?
extra_html:
Drop the teacher

The first move is to stop running the teacher at all during training. Instead, the teacher's top-K logits are computed once and cached, and the student trains against that cache. The authors report this offline setup matching online distillation at near-identical training loss, while freeing the teacher's memory: about 29% faster per iteration and up to 41% higher throughput on a single H200 GPU.

Stop materializing the logit tensor

The second move targets the loss itself. A standard KL objective builds a full vocabulary-sized logit tensor, and that spike is what caps how long a sequence you can train on. Their fused, chunked KL loss never materializes it, so peak memory becomes linear in sequence length — enough to train at four times the context (32,768 tokens) on one GPU. A separate output-head-only benchmark isolates the kernel and confirms the scaling from 4K to 256K tokens. Together, the two changes make large-scale healing runs and hundreds of ablations affordable; the chunked-loss implementation is released on GitHub. See the paper for the supporting ablations on loss design and sequence packing.

related.title: Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network
related.hook: A big model's softened probabilities say more than hard labels - they reveal how classes relate, so training a small model to mimic them transfers knowledge a one-hot target never could.

related.title: DistilBERT: Smaller, Faster, Cheaper, Lighter
related.hook: Distill during pre-training instead of after, and you get a general-purpose language model that is 40% smaller and 60% faster while keeping 97% of BERT's understanding.

related.title: Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training
related.hook: On-policy self-distillation was supposed to fight forgetting in continual post-training — instead, denser self-distillation can drift further off course and collapse outright.

flashcards.prompt: What does 'offline' knowledge distillation mean here, and why does it save resources?
flashcards.back_html: The teacher's top-K logits are computed once and cached, then the student trains against that cache. The teacher never sits in GPU memory during training, which the authors report as ~29% faster per iteration at near-identical loss.

flashcards.prompt: Why does a fused, chunked KL loss let you train at much longer context on one GPU?

choices.text: It never materializes the full vocabulary-sized logit tensor, so peak memory grows linearly with sequence length
It reduces the vocabulary size by pruning rare tokens before training
It offloads the loss computation to CPU memory between steps

flashcards.explanation_html: The usual memory spike comes from holding a [sequence x vocabulary] logit tensor. Chunking the loss and fusing the kernel avoids that materialization, letting the authors train at 32,768 tokens on a single GPU.

flashcards.prompt: Why is the distillation step so important when building a small deployable model?
flashcards.back_html: Small models are rarely trained from scratch — they're compressed from a larger one and then 'healed' by distillation. That recovery step largely determines the final quality, so its cost limits how many ablations you can afford.
